summary: Supply the specific volume, the volumetric flow rate, the mass flow rate and the enthalphy and the Mixed air calculator solves for vapour pressure (Pv1). Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Mixed air calculator work?
sections.html:
The Mixed air calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports vapour pressure (Pv1) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the specific volume (v1), the volumetric flow rate (V2), the mass flow rate (m2) and the enthalphy (h3).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mixed air calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Vapour pressure (pv 1)=200000 × humidity ratio (ω1) × mixing pressure (Pa) ÷ (200000 × humidity ratio (ω1) + 124389)
Humidity ratio (ω2)=-124389 × vapour pressure (Pv2) ÷ (200000 × vapour pressure (Pv2) − 200000 × mixing pressure (Pa))
Vapour pressure (pv 3)=200000 × humidity ratio (ω3) × mixing pressure (Pa) ÷ (200000 × humidity ratio (ω3) + 124389)
A=the natural log of ((625 ÷ 382) × vapour pressure (Pv1))
Vapour pressure (pv 2)=(382 ÷ 625) × the exponential of (A2)
Vapour pressure (pv 3)=(382 ÷ 625) × the exponential of (A3)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Mixing pressure (Pa) = 10 kPa and Humidity ratio (ω1) = 10 g. The calculator returns Dew point temperature (tdp 1) = 296 °C and Vapour pressure (pv 1) = 9.4145 kPa.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Dew point temperature (tdp 1) = 296 °C and Vapour pressure (pv 1) = 9.4145 kPa should be roughly the size you expected from Mixing pressure (Pa) = 10 kPa and Humidity ratio (ω1) = 10 g.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals
  • Flow rate, opening in cubic meters per minute
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • %, opening in percent
  • Mass, opening in grams
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Pressure, opening in kilopascals
  • Volume per mass, opening in cubic meters per kilogram

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Mixed air calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the specific volume, the volumetric flow rate and the mass flow rate — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Mixed air calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns vapour pressure (Pv1), derived from the specific volume, the volumetric flow rate and the mass flow rate. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Mixed air calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the specific volume, the volumetric flow rate, the mass flow rate and the enthalphy, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mixing pressure (Pa) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mixing pressure (Pa) opens in kilopascals and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Dew point temperature (tdp 1) = 296 °C. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Mixed air calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
